passage:
'Sarika, hi. I got us both cold coffee.'
'I only have twenty minutes.'
'That's fine.' Lavanya sat across from her in the college canteen they used to skip lectures in. 'You look tired.'
'I'm fine. We're doing important work.'
'I believe you. What kind of work?'
'You wouldn't understand. People outside are asleep.'
Lavanya took a sip and let that sit. She wanted to say, That's a line, you didn't used to talk like this. She didn't. 'Okay. Maybe I don't understand. I'd like to.'
'That's what they said you'd do. Act interested.'
'I'm not acting. I miss you. That's all.'
Sarika looked at the table. Her thumb rubbed the edge of the cup.
'I have to go.'
'Okay. Same time next month? I'll bring the coffee.'
Sarika hesitated at the door. 'Maybe.'
Lavanya watched her go and didn't follow.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya and Sarika meet?
qa.a: They met in the college canteen they used to skip lectures in.

qa.q: What did Lavanya want to say but didn't, and why?
qa.a: Lavanya was tempted to point out that Sarika was repeating a line, but held back because she misses Sarika and was worried that mocking her would push her further away.

qa.q: Why is Lavanya's calm, open-door approach wise at this stage?
qa.a: It keeps trust alive, so when Sarika's doubts grow she will have someone safe to come back to.

qa.q: What might Sarika's thumb rubbing the cup suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she may be more unsettled than her stock replies show, perhaps moved by being missed.

grounding: It shows a friend reaching out and meeting defensive stock replies, but staying calm, avoiding ridicule and keeping the door open.

passage:
The first time I tried to talk to Shreya about the group, I made a mess of it. I said, 'Beta, these people are using you.' She stood up, said, 'Mummy, you sound exactly like they said you would,' and left. She didn't call for two months.
I'm her mother. I wanted to argue, to send articles, to cry at her. My sister told me to threaten to cut her off.
I didn't. I sent a message every Sunday instead. Nothing heavy. 'Made your favourite rasam today.' 'The neem tree is flowering.' She read them. She didn't reply.
When she did come home for Diwali, I didn't bring it up. When she said something that sounded like a slogan, I said, 'Hm. Tell me more,' and meant it.
She's still with them. But last week she asked, very quietly, if her old room was still there.
It is. I told her so.
— Manjula

qa.q: What did Manjula message Shreya every Sunday?
qa.a: Manjula sent a message every Sunday, nothing heavy, like 'Made your favourite rasam today.'

qa.q: What might Shreya's question about her old room suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It may suggest that doubts are starting to grow and she wants to know there is a safe place to come back to.

qa.q: What did Manjula change after the first conversation went wrong?
qa.a: She stopped accusing and arguing, stayed calm, kept regular gentle contact, and listened when Shreya repeated slogans, which kept trust alive.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt receiving small messages every Sunday without pressure?
qa.a: Shreya may have felt quietly loved and not attacked, which made it easier to ask about coming home.

grounding: It shows a mother reaching out, meeting a defensive stock reply, and then staying calm, avoiding ridicule and keeping the door open.
